claim: Sarcomere morphology is remarkably conserved from fruit flies to humans
source: Sarcomere morphology is remarkably conserved from fruit flies to humans: each sarcomere is bordered by two Z-discs that cross-link the plus-ends of parallel actin filaments, while their minus ends face towards the centrally located bipolar myosin filaments (Lange et al., 2006; Lemke and Schnorrer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lange et al., 2006; Lemke and Schnorrer, 2017) and represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Titin binds with its N-terminus to α-actinin at the Z-disc and is embedded with its C-terminus at the M-band of the sarcomere in mammals
source: Both filaments are stably linked by the gigantic titin spring protein, which in mammals binds with its N-terminus to α-actinin at the Z-disc and is embedded with its C-terminus at the M-band of the sarcomere.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about mammalian titin structure and function.

claim: Titin determines the length of the mammalian sarcomere
source: Thus, titin determines the length of the mammalian sarcomere (Linke, 2018; Luis and Schnorrer, 2021; Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Drosophila is an excellent model to study how a sarcomere is built during development
source: As sarcomere architecture is well-conserved, Drosophila is an excellent model to study how a sarcomere is built during development (Katzemich et al., 2013; Katzemich et al., 2015; Orfanos et al., 2015; Weitkunat et al., 2017; Weitkunat et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies and is based on the inference from conserved sarcomere architecture.

claim: Generation of monoclonal antibodies against Drosophila sarcomere proteins has been helpful to locate key proteins within the mature sarcomere
source: Generation of monoclonal antibodies against Drosophila sarcomere proteins has been helpful to locate key proteins within the mature sarcomere (Burkart et al., 2007; Ferguson et al., 1994; Katzemich et al., 2012; Lakey et al., 1990; Qiu et al., 2005; Szikora et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies that used antibodies for protein localization.

claim: There is no comprehensive toolbox of antibodies recognising defined domains of the large sarcomeric proteins in Drosophila
source: However, to date, there is no comprehensive toolbox of antibodies recognising defined domains of the large sarcomeric proteins, in particular against defined domains of the two large Drosophila titin homologs, Sallimus (Sls) and Projectin (gene called bent, bt).
evidence: This claim represents a gap in existing research tools as stated by the authors.

claim: A number of GFP-tagged Drosophila sarcomeric protein lines label only a subset of protein isoforms or result in homozygous loss of function phenotypes
source: Nevertheless, a number of these tagged lines label only a subset of protein isoforms or result in homozygous loss of function phenotypes as the GFP-tagged protein cannot fully support the function of the endogenous protein in the dense sarcomeric environment (O'Donnell et al., 1989; Orfanos and Sparrow, 2013; Orfanos et al., 2015; Sarov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies documenting limitations of GFP-tagging approaches.

claim: Nanobodies are approximately 4 nm in size and 12-15 kDa in molecular weight
source: We chose the recent camelid nanobody technology because of the small size of the nanobodies (~4 nm, 12–15 kDa), their single-chain protein nature, and their potentially high affinity against target domains (Muyldermans, 2013; Pleiner et al., 2018; Pleiner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing nanobody properties.

claim: Nanobodies can be used on fixed samples or fused to a fluorescent protein and expressed in living tissues
source: As nanobodies can be used on fixed samples or fused to a fluorescent protein and expressed in living tissues, nanobodies are ideal tools to quantify the position and dynamics of sarcomeric proteins in their dense environment.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about nanobody applications and is supported by inference about their utility.

claim: Application of nanobodies to the Drosophila model has been largely restricted to commercially available GFP and mCherry nanobodies
source: Thus far, the application of nanobodies to the Drosophila model has been largely restricted to commercially available GFP and mCherry nanobodies that allowed localisation, trapping, or degradation of GFP-tagged or mCherry-tagged proteins in Drosophila tissue (Ákos et al., 2021; Caussinus et al., 2011; Harmansa and Affolter, 2018; Harmansa et al., 2017; Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies using GFP and mCherry nanobodies in Drosophila.

claim: Nanobodies that recognise endogenous Drosophila protein domains have not been reported prior to this study
source: However, nanobodies that recognise endogenous Drosophila protein domains have not been reported.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature as stated by the authors.

claim: The study generated a nanobody toolbox against seven different epitopes of the two Drosophila titin homologs, Sallimus and Projectin
source: Here we generated a nanobody toolbox against seven different epitopes of the two Drosophila titin homologs, Sallimus (Sls) and Projectin (Proj).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents a primary finding of the study.

claim: The study raised nanobodies against two epitopes of the core M-band protein Obscurin
source: Additionally, we raised nanobodies against two epitopes of the core M-band protein Obscurin and against epitopes of the key Z-disc proteins α-Actinin and Zasp52.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents a primary finding of the study.

claim: The nanobodies show superior penetration and labelling efficiencies compared to antibodies
source: We verified their specificity as well as their superior penetration and labelling efficiencies compared to antibodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A gigantic Sallimus isoform stretches more than 2 µm to bridge the sarcomeric I-band in larval muscles
source: By applying our toolbox to larval muscles, we found a gigantic Sallimus isoform stretching more than 2 µm to bridge the sarcomeric I-band, while Projectin covers almost the entire myosin filaments in a polar orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the nanobody toolbox.

claim: Projectin covers almost the entire myosin filaments in a polar orientation
source: By applying our toolbox to larval muscles, we found a gigantic Sallimus isoform stretching more than 2 µm to bridge the sarcomeric I-band, while Projectin covers almost the entire myosin filaments in a polar orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the nanobody toolbox.

claim: Transgenic expression of tagged nanobodies confirmed their high affinity-binding without affecting target protein function
source: Transgenic expression of tagged nanobodies confirmed their high affinity-binding without affecting target protein function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic fly lines.

claim: Expression of anti-Sallimus nanobodies with degradation signals caused developmental lethality
source: Finally, adding a degradation signal to anti-Sallimus nanobodies suggested that it is difficult to fully degrade Sallimus in mature sarcomeres; however, expression of these nanobodies caused developmental lethality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deGrad experiments.

claim: It is difficult to fully degrade Sallimus in mature sarcomeres
source: Finally, adding a degradation signal to anti-Sallimus nanobodies suggested that it is difficult to fully degrade Sallimus in mature sarcomeres; however, expression of these nanobodies caused developmental lethality.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations with deGrad nanobodies.

claim: The longest Sallimus isoform contains 48 immunoglobulin domains of the total 52 Ig domains coded in the Sls gene
source: The longest Sls isoform contains 48 immunoglobulin (Ig) domains of the total 52 Ig domains coded in the Sls gene (four are selectively present in a short larval isoform).
evidence: This claim is based on annotation of Flybase expression database data.

claim: Sallimus contains long stretches of flexible regions rich in amino acids proline, valine, glutamic acid, and lysine (PEVK) that form an elastic spring
source: Additionally, Sls contains long stretches of flexible regions rich in amino acids proline, valine, glutamic acid, and lysine (PEVK) that form an elastic spring as well as five C-terminal fibronectin (Fn) domains.
evidence: This claim is based on protein domain annotation and established knowledge about PEVK regions.

claim: Long PEVK stretches are not expressed in flight muscles resulting in a short indirect flight muscle Sallimus isoform
source: In flight muscles, these long PEVK stretches are, however, not expressed resulting in a short indirect flight muscle Sls isoform (Figure 1A; Burkart et al., 2007; Spletter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The Sallimus domain organisation largely resembles the I-band part of mammalian titin
source: This domain organisation largely resembles the I-band part of mammalian titin (Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published literature on mammalian titin structure.

claim: The long Projectin isoform contains 35 Ig and 39 Fn domains organized mainly in Ig-Fn super-repeats
source: Conversely, the long Projectin isoform contains 35 Ig and 39 Fn domains that are organised mainly in Ig-Fn super-repeats with a consensus myosin light chain kinase domain close to its C-terminus (Figure 1B; Ayme-Southgate et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on protein domain annotation supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The Projectin domain organisation largely resembles the A-band part of mammalian titin
source: This domain organisation largely resembles the A-band part of mammalian titin (Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published literature on mammalian titin structure.

claim: Sls-Nano2, Sls-Nano39, Sls-Nano42, and Sls-Nano48 were successfully generated against selected Sallimus domains
source: We successfully expressed Sls-Ig13/14, Sls-Ig49/50, and Sls-Ig51-Fn2 recombinantly and generated the respective nanobodies Sls-Nano2, Sls-Nano39, Sls-Nano42, and Sls-Nano48 against these domains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents experimental results illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Projectin nanobodies Proj-Nano30, Proj-Nano28 and 29, Proj-Nano33, and Proj-Nano34, 35, 37, and 46 were generated against selected Projectin domains
source: For Projectin, we selected Ig5-8, Fn1/2, and Ig27-Fn35 as well as the kinase domain to generate Projectin nanobodies Proj-Nano30, Proj-Nano28 and 29, Proj-Nano33, and Proj-Nano34, 35, 37, and 46 that recognise these domains, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents experimental results illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Nanobodies Obs-Nano55, 56, and 57 were raised against the N-terminal SH-3/RhoGEF domain of Obscurin
source: In a complementary approach to both titins, we also selected two regions in the core M-band protein Obscurin (gene called Unc-89), namely, the N-terminal SH-3/RhoGEF and the middle Ig13-17, to raise the nanobodies Obs-Nano55, 56, and 57, and Obs-Nano58 and 59, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents experimental results illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Nanobodies Obs-Nano58 and 59 were raised against the middle Ig13-17 domain of Obscurin
source: In a complementary approach to both titins, we also selected two regions in the core M-band protein Obscurin (gene called Unc-89), namely, the N-terminal SH-3/RhoGEF and the middle Ig13-17, to raise the nanobodies Obs-Nano55, 56, and 57, and Obs-Nano58 and 59, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents experimental results illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Nanobodies Actn-Nano62, 63, and 64 were generated against the CH1-Spectrin4 domains of α-Actinin
source: Furthermore, we expressed full-length α-Actinin to generate nanobodies against its CH1-Spectrin4 domains, named Actn-Nano62, 63, and 64, as well as nanobodies recognising the PDZ domain of the core Z-disc component Zasp52, called Zasp52-Nano65 and 66 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents experimental results illustrated in Figures 1D and E.

claim: Nanobodies Zasp52-Nano65 and 66 were generated against the PDZ domain of Zasp52
source: Furthermore, we expressed full-length α-Actinin to generate nanobodies against its CH1-Spectrin4 domains, named Actn-Nano62, 63, and 64, as well as nanobodies recognising the PDZ domain of the core Z-disc component Zasp52, called Zasp52-Nano65 and 66 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and represents experimental results illustrated in Figures 1D and E.

claim: Indirect flight muscles from 1000 wild-type adult flies were used for alpaca immunization
source: First, we hand-dissected the indirect flight muscles from 1000 wild-type adult flies and isolated their myofibrils, which express large amounts of the selected target domains (Spletter et al., 2018). These were used for two immunisations of a single alpaca.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: A phage display library with a complexity of more than 10^8 independent clones was constructed
source: Finally, a phage display library with a complexity of more than 108 independent clones was constructed.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and results.

claim: Three rounds of phage display were employed using low concentrations (0.1–1 nM) of baits to isolate high-affinity nanobodies
source: To isolate high-affinity nanobodies, we employed three rounds of phage display, using low concentrations (0.1–1 nM) of baits.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology used for nanobody selection.

claim: Typical yields of nanobody purification were 20–50 mg per litre bacterial culture
source: Selected clones were then expressed as His14-SUMO-tagged or His14-NEDD8-tagged fusions in E. coli and purified by the affinity-capture-protease elution strategy (Frey and Görlich, 2014a), with typical yields of 20–50 mg nanobody per litre bacterial culture.
evidence: This claim describes experimental results for nanobody production yields.

claim: Nanobody labelling with fluorophore maleimides was almost quantitative
source: Using this workflow, labelling was almost quantitative, as indicated by the size shifts on sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) (Figure 3A) and by a ratiometric measurement of the optical densities at the absorption maxima of protein and the fluorophore.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sls-Nano2 binds to Sls Ig13/14 domains with a KD in the 10 pM range
source: The data indicate a nearly irreversible binding with an on-rate of ~106·M–1·s–1, an off-rate in the order of 10–5·M–1·s–1 and KD in the 10 pM range.
evidence: This claim is supported by biolayer interferometry measurements described in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The high affinity of nanobodies can be explained by Drosophila proteins being highly immunogenic in mammals, the very large immune repertoire of alpacas, and stringent selection from a very large immune library
source: The high affinity can be explained by Drosophila proteins being highly immunogenic in mammals, by the very large immune repertoire of alpacas, and by our particularly stringent selection from a very large immune library.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations and known properties of the immunization system.

claim: Most anti-Sallimus and anti-Projectin nanobodies efficiently stained embryonic muscles showing the expected striated pattern in stage 17 embryos
source: Most of our nanobodies efficiently stained embryonic muscles, showing the expected striated pattern of Sls and Projectin in stage 17 embryos (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: In total, 12 different Sallimus and Projectin nanobodies were generated against three different Sls and four different Projectin epitopes
source: Thus, in total, we generated 12 different Sls and Projectin nanobodies against three different Sls and four different Projectin epitopes.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental results of nanobody generation.

claim: Staining of Sallimus or Projectin was severely reduced after muscle-specific RNAi knock-down of the respective protein
source: We found that in all cases the staining of Sls or Projectin was severely reduced after the knock-down of the respective protein, demonstrating the specificity of our nanobodies (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: Both Sallimus and Projectin are required to generate striated sarcomeres in stage 17 embryos
source: In each case, we found that the striated pattern of the other protein was lost, demonstrating that both Sls and Projectin are required to generate striated sarcomeres in stage 17 embryos.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations in RNAi experiments.

claim: All five anti-Obscurin nanobodies specifically label the M-band in flight muscles
source: We found that all five different nanobodies that we generated either against the N-terminal SH3-RhoGEF domains (Obs-Nano55, 56, 57) or against the central Ig13-17 domains of Obscurin (Obs-Nano58, 59) specifically label the M-band (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), as had been described with established antibodies or GFP fusions (Katzemich et al., 2015; Sarov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures, and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Anti-Obscurin nanobody localization is strongly reduced or absent in the hypomorphic Obscurin allele Unc-89[EY15484]
source: This localisation is strongly reduced or absent in the hypomorphic Obscurin allele Unc-89[EY15484] (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating the specificity of the anti-Obscurin nanobodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant analysis shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Anti-α-Actinin nanobodies show Z-disc localization that is lost upon muscle-specific RNAi of α-Actinin
source: Muscle-specific RNAi of α-Actinin results in larval lethality (Schnorrer et al., 2010), with strongly reduced α-Actinin signal at the Z-disc, showing the specificity of our three new nanobodies (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B and supplementary figures.

claim: The Z-disc signal of both anti-Zasp52 nanobodies is specifically lost upon muscle-specific RNAi of Zasp52
source: Similarly, we found that the Z-disc signal of both anti-Zasp52 nanobodies is specifically lost upon muscle-specific RNAi of Zasp52 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: All 22 novel nanobodies against 11 different domains result in specific detection of the target protein in muscle tissue
source: Taken together, we conclude that all our 22 novel nanobodies against 11 different domains result in specific detection of the target protein in muscle tissue.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental validation results for all generated nanobodies.

claim: Nanobodies are only 13 kDa and approximately 4 nm in size
source: Nanobodies are only 13 kDa and ~4 nm in size (Helma et al., 2015; Pleiner et al., 2015), making it ideal to place a label close to the domain of interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on nanobody properties.

claim: The Sls-Nano2 intensity decay over z-depth is about 2.5-fold less than that of the anti-Sls antibody label
source: Using the same imaging conditions and the same fluorophore for Sls-Nano2 and the combination of anti-Sls primary and secondary antibodies, we found that the Sls-Nano2 intensity decay over z-depth is about 2.5-fold less than that of the anti-Sls antibody label (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Sls-Nano2 readily diffuses into thick flight muscle samples, whereas the Sls antibody is limited to the top layer of myofibrils
source: We found that Sls-Nano2 readily diffuses into the thick flight muscle samples, whereas the Sls antibody is limited to the top layer of myofibrils (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6 supplementary figures.

claim: Nanobodies stained the body muscles of stage 17 embryos well, while anti-Sls, Mhc, and Projectin antibodies did not produce good staining patterns
source: While our nanobodies stained the body muscles of stage 17 embryos well, which displayed the striated pattern of the first formed sarcomeres, neither anti-Sls (anti-Kettin), Mhc, nor Projectin antibodies produced a good staining pattern (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative staining data shown in Figure 6 supplementary figures.

claim: The generated nanobody toolbox allows efficient labelling of sarcomeres in large flight muscles or whole-mount late-stage embryos
source: Together, we conclude that the here generated nanobody toolbox allows efficient labelling of sarcomeres in large flight muscles or whole-mount late-stage embryos.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations of nanobody performance.

claim: Flight muscles contain a very short approximately 100 nm wide I-band
source: This pattern is expected since flight muscles contain a very short ~100 nm wide I-band (Burkart et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on flight muscle structure.

claim: The Sls-Nano42 band has a smaller cross-sectional radius compared to Sls-Nano2 in flight muscles
source: The Sls-Nano42 band has a smaller cross-sectional radius compared to Sls-Nano2, suggesting that Sls-Ig51-Fn2 is not present in all the Sls isoforms expressed during the final stages of myofibril maturation that complete radial myofibril growth (González-Morales et al., 2019; Spletter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and inference about isoform expression.

claim: Staining for the N-terminal portion of Projectin Ig5-8 with Proj-Nano30 resulted in a single band overlapping with the Z-disc in flight muscles
source: Next, we investigated the localisation of Projectin in flight muscles and found that staining for the N-terminal portion of Ig5-8 with Proj-Nano30 resulted in a single band overlapping with the Z-disc, whereas Proj-Nano37, which recognises the Projectin kinase domain at its C-terminal end, resulted in two bands right and left of the I-band, likely overlapping with the myosin filament (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Proj-Nano37 recognizing the Projectin kinase domain resulted in two bands right and left of the I-band in flight muscles
source: Next, we investigated the localisation of Projectin in flight muscles and found that staining for the N-terminal portion of Ig5-8 with Proj-Nano30 resulted in a single band overlapping with the Z-disc, whereas Proj-Nano37, which recognises the Projectin kinase domain at its C-terminal end, resulted in two bands right and left of the I-band, likely overlapping with the myosin filament (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Anti-Projectin nanobodies established that Projectin is oriented linearly in flight muscles, with its N-terminus closer to the Z-disc and its C-terminus facing the myosin filaments
source: Hence, the anti-Projectin nanobodies established that Projectin is oriented linearly in flight muscles, with its N-terminus being closer to the Z-disc and its C-terminus facing the myosin filaments.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations with multiple nanobodies.

claim: Drosophila leg or larval muscles have longer I-bands compared to flight muscles, likely caused by expression of longer Sallimus splice isoforms that include large parts of the flexible PEVK spring domains
source: In contrast to flight muscles, Drosophila leg or larval muscles have longer I-bands, likely caused by the expression of longer Sls splice isoforms that include large parts of the flexible PEVK spring domains, making these muscles softer (Burkart et al., 2007; Spletter and Schnorrer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural observations and is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sls-Nano2 signal overlaps with the Z-disc in leg and larval muscles
source: The Sls-Nano2 signal overlaps with the Z-disc in leg and larval muscles, similar to flight muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data.

claim: Sls-Nano42 recognizing Sls-Ig51-Fn2 showed two distinct bands with larger distances in larval muscles compared to leg muscles
source: However, Sls-Nano42, which recognises the C-terminal portion of Sls-Ig51-Fn2, showed two distinct bands with larger distances in larval muscles compared to leg muscles (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figures 7B and C.

claim: Drosophila Sallimus is extended as a linear molecule bridging from the Z-disc likely to the myosin filament in sarcomeres with long I-bands
source: This demonstrates that Drosophila Sls is extended as a linear molecule bridging from the Z-disc likely to the myosin filament in sarcomeres with long I-bands.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations with nanobodies.

claim: Staining of adult leg or larval body muscles with N- and C-terminal Projectin nanobodies showed two large blocks located on the myosin filaments
source: Consistent with these reports, staining of adult leg or larval body muscles with nanobodies that recognise the N- and C-terminal portions of Projectin, Proj-Nano30, and Proj-Nano37, respectively, showed two large blocks, instead of sharp bands located on the myosin filaments in both adult leg and larval body muscles (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figures 7B and C and is consistent with published reports.

claim: Projectin decorates the myosin filaments of cross-striated Drosophila muscles
source: These results demonstrate that Projectin decorates the myosin filaments of cross-striated Drosophila muscles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Anti-α-Actinin and anti-Zasp52 nanobodies detect their targets at the Z-disc of larval muscle sarcomeres
source: As expected, we found that our nanobodies are detecting α-Actinin and Zasp52 at the Z-disc of larval muscle sarcomeres (Figure 7D), the well-established location for these core Z-disc components (Jani and Schöck, 2007; Schnorrer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Anti-Obscurin nanobodies recognizing the central Obs-Ig13-17 domains show the expected M-band pattern in larval muscle
source: More surprisingly, we found that anti-Obscurin nanobodies recognising the central Obs-Ig13-17 domains show the expected M-band pattern; however, the ones recognising the N-terminal Obs-SH3-RhoGEF domains show no staining in larval muscle (Figure 7D), while they do show the expected pattern in flight muscles (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figures 7D and 5A.

claim: Anti-Obscurin nanobodies recognizing the N-terminal Obs-SH3-RhoGEF domains show no staining in larval muscle
source: More surprisingly, we found that anti-Obscurin nanobodies recognising the central Obs-Ig13-17 domains show the expected M-band pattern; however, the ones recognising the N-terminal Obs-SH3-RhoGEF domains show no staining in larval muscle (Figure 7D), while they do show the expected pattern in flight muscles (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figures 7D and 5A.

claim: A shorter Obscurin isoform missing the N-terminal SH3 and RhoGEF domains is specifically expressed in larval muscles
source: This suggests that the shorter Obscurin isoform annotated in Flybase (see Figure 1C) is specifically expressed in larval muscles. This matches with whole larval transcriptomics data of Obscurin (http://flybase.org/reports/FBgn0053519).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations and is supported by transcriptomics data from Flybase.

claim: Sallimus extends over more than 2 µm in relaxed L3 sarcomeres that are about 8.5 µm long
source: We found that Sls extends over more than 2 µm in relaxed L3 sarcomeres that are about 8.5 µm long (Figure 8A) and thus Sls is extended longer than the human titin protein in skeletal muscle (Linke, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 8A and comparison with published literature.

claim: Sls-Nano42 localises Sls-Ig51-Fn2 to the beginning of the myosin filaments in larval muscles
source: Indeed, we found that Sls-Nano42 localises Sls-Ig51-Fn2 to the beginning of the myosin filaments, demonstrating that each long Sls isoform indeed stretches across the entire long I-band of larval muscles, likely to mechanically link the Z-discs to the myosin filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental co-staining data with anti-Mhc antibody.

claim: Each long Sallimus isoform stretches across the entire long I-band of larval muscles, likely to mechanically link the Z-discs to the myosin filaments
source: Indeed, we found that Sls-Nano42 localises Sls-Ig51-Fn2 to the beginning of the myosin filaments, demonstrating that each long Sls isoform indeed stretches across the entire long I-band of larval muscles, likely to mechanically link the Z-discs to the myosin filaments.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: N-terminal and C-terminal Projectin nanobody staining blocks were slightly shifted with respect to each other in larval muscles
source: When carefully analysing the overlap of Proj-Nano30 and Proj-Nano37 staining, we surprisingly found that these blocks were slightly shifted with respect to each other. N-terminal Proj-Nano30 staining was located closer towards the Z-disc, whereas the C-terminal Proj-Nano37 staining was closer towards the M-band (see Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figures 7B and C.

claim: The small central gap visible in the Projectin kinase domain nanobody patterns is caused by a Projectin-free M-band of the larval sarcomere
source: We hypothesised that the small central gap visible in the Projectin kinase domain nanobody patterns is caused by a Projectin-free M-band of the larval sarcomere. Co-labelling the M-band with our anti-Obscurin nanobody Obs-Nano58 confirmed that the gap present in the Proj-kinase nanobody pattern is consistent with its absence from the M-band (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is based on hypothesis testing with experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Projectin decorates the myosin filaments in a defined polar orientation, likely from the tip of the myosin filaments until the beginning of the H-zone
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that Projectin decorates the myosin filaments in a defined polar orientation, likely from the tip of the myosin filaments until the beginning of the H-zone that is devoid of myosin heads (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations and is illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: Expression of Sls-Nano2-NeonGreen with Mef2-GAL4 driver results in normal sarcomere morphology and Sallimus protein length
source: We expressed the nanobodies with the muscle-specific Mef2-GAL4 driver and fixed the larvae to assay the morphology of larval muscles with anti-Sls nanobodies Sls-Nano2 and Sls-Nano42. We found that the sarcomere morphology and the length of the Sls protein are normal (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 supplementary figures.

claim: Larvae expressing Sls-Nano2-NeonGreen move with comparable speed and persistence as controls
source: We found that larvae expressing Sls-Nano2-NeonGreen during muscle development move with a comparable speed and persistence as controls (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C, D, Figure 9—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative locomotion analysis shown in Figure 9 supplementary figures.

claim: Sls-Nano2-NeonGreen binds to Sls-Ig13/14 in vivo
source: We found the expected striated pattern of Sls-Nano2-NeonGreen labelling a single thin stripe, resembling the Sls-Nano2 staining in fixed larval muscles (Figure 9A). We conclude that Sls-Nano2-NeonGreen binds to Sls-Ig13/14 in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from live imaging data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Sls-Nano2 is stably bound to Sls-Ig13/14 target in living larval muscles
source: We found very little recovery during the observation period. This demonstrates that the Sls-Nano2 is indeed stably bound to Sls-Ig13/14 target and that Sls protein does not exchange significantly over a 30-min period in mature larval muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: Sallimus protein does not exchange significantly over a 30-min period in mature larval muscles
source: We found very little recovery during the observation period. This demonstrates that the Sls-Nano2 is indeed stably bound to Sls-Ig13/14 target and that Sls protein does not exchange significantly over a 30-min period in mature larval muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: Expression of Sls-Nano2-deGrad under Mef2-GAL4 control reduced the fluorescent signal of Sls-Nano2 (Ig13/14) by approximately 80% compared to control larvae
source: When expressing Sls-Nano2-deGrad under Mef2-GAL4 control in larval muscles from embryonic stages onwards, we found in stainings that the fluorescent signal of labelled Sls-Nano2 (Ig13/14) was reduced by ~80% as compared to control larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative staining intensity measurements.

claim: Expression of Sls-Nano2-deGrad in muscles caused lethality at the pupal stage with no adults eclosing
source: We found that expression of Sls-Nano2-deGrad in muscles caused a drastic phenotype later in development, namely lethality at the pupal stage; no adults were eclosing (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The majority of Sls-Nano42-deGrad expressing pupae died, with much fewer than the expected 50% of adults eclosing
source: Similarly, the majority of the Sls-Nano42-deGrad expressing pupae died, since much fewer than the expected 50% of adults eclosed from the cross of the heterozygous line to the Mef2-GAL4 driver (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The few surviving Sls-Nano42-deGrad adults showed variable myofibril thickness, which is never found in wild type
source: In addition, we observed a variable myofibril thickness in the few surviving Sls-Nano42-deGrad adults, which is never found in wild type (Figure 10D), pointing to a specific defect in myofibril maturation that might be controlled by Sls availability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 10D and inference about the cause.

claim: High affinity to target epitopes is likely the case for most members of the nanobody toolbox
source: High affinity to the target epitopes is likely the case for most members of the here presented nanobody toolbox, as exemplified in detail for Sls-Nano2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the detailed characterization of Sls-Nano2.

claim: Mammalian titin was suggested to be surprisingly dynamic at least in in vitro cultured cardiomyocytes
source: It will be interesting to extend these studies to longer time frames as mammalian titin was suggested to be surprisingly dynamic at least in in vitro cultured cardiomyocytes (Rudolph et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Sarcomeres are very dense structures that likely exclude most soluble proteins
source: Given that sarcomeres are very dense structures that likely exclude most soluble proteins (O'Donnell et al., 1989), it is hard to imagine how 26S proteasomes can gain access.
evidence: This claim is based on inference supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Targeting a single degron to Sallimus does not suffice for complete degradation
source: It is thus perhaps not surprising that targeting a single degron to Sallimus does not suffice for a complete degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations with deGrad nanobodies.

claim: The small size of nanobodies places possible labels very close to their target epitopes
source: The small size of nanobodies not only allows superior penetration into tissues as shown here for late-stage Drosophila embryos or thick flight muscle tissue but also places possible labels very close to their target epitopes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known size of nanobodies and experimental observations.

claim: Most Sallimus isoforms present in flight muscles contain the C-terminal Sls-Ig51-Fn2 domains
source: Our data suggest that most of the Sls isoforms present in flight muscles do contain the C-terminal Sls-Ig51-Fn2 domains. This is consistent with developmental transcriptomics results that included splice isoform annotations (Spletter et al., 2015; Spletter et al., 2018), and the very low expression of a Sls isoform that uses an early alternative stop codon, which is rather expressed in leg muscles (Sarov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and is supported by citations to transcriptomics studies.

claim: Most Sallimus isoforms have at least the potential to bridge to the myosin filament in flight muscles
source: Our new nanobodies now clarify that most Sls isoforms have at least the potential to bridge to the myosin filament in flight muscles (Schueder et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and is supported by citation to an accompanying manuscript.

claim: Larval muscles are considered soft compared to stiff flight muscles
source: Larval muscles are considered soft compared to stiff flight muscles.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Larval sarcomeres have a relaxed length of about 8.5 µm and can contract up to about 4.5 µm
source: This is consistent with their large dynamic length range: larval sarcomeres have a relaxed length of about 8.5 µm and can contract up to about 4.5 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Flight muscle sarcomeres only contract 3.5% of their length during flight, about 120 nm
source: In contrast, flight muscle sarcomeres only contract 3.5% of their length during flight, about 120 nm (measured in Drosophila virilis Chan and Dickinson, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published measurements.

claim: The I-band of relaxed larval muscles is long, about 2 µm
source: Consistent with this, the I-band of relaxed larval muscles is long, about 2 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Mammalian titin is 1.5 µm long in 3 µm long relaxed human sarcomeres
source: However, this finding still comes as a significant surprise, since the mammalian titin is considered to be the 'longest' protein in the animal kingdom; however, it is 'only' 1.5 µm long in 3 µm long relaxed human sarcomeres (Linke, 2018; Llewellyn et al., 2008; Regev et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on mammalian titin.

claim: Mammalian titin is the largest protein by molecular weight (up to 3800 kDa)
source: Mammalian titin is certainly the largest protein by molecular weight (up to 3800 kDa) (Brynnel et al., 2018), whereas the longest predicted Drosophila Sls isoform has a mass of 'only' 2100 kDa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The longest predicted Drosophila Sallimus isoform has a mass of 2100 kDa
source: Mammalian titin is certainly the largest protein by molecular weight (up to 3800 kDa) (Brynnel et al., 2018), whereas the longest predicted Drosophila Sls isoform has a mass of 'only' 2100 kDa.
evidence: This claim is based on prediction from sequence data.

claim: Drosophila Sallimus is likely under strong mechanical tension in larval muscles with its long PEVK spring domains likely unfolded
source: The long extension of Sls found here makes it likely that Sls is under strong mechanical tension in larval muscles, and hence its long PEVK spring domains are likely unfolded to allow bridging of the long I-band in the relaxed state of the larval muscle (model in Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations and mechanical considerations.

claim: Drosophila Sallimus may store a significant amount of energy for the next round of muscle contraction by unfolding its PEVK domains
source: Such, Drosophila Sls may store a significant amount of energy for the next round of muscle contraction, purely by unfolding its PEVK domains and not necessarily needing to unfold any of its Ig domains, the latter has recently been suggested for mammalian titin (Rivas-Pardo et al., 2016; Rivas-Pardo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from structural observations and comparison with mammalian titin.

claim: Insect Sallimus might be one of the 'longest' proteins naturally occurring in animals
source: Hence, our data identify that insect Sls might indeed be one of the 'longest' proteins naturally occurring in animals, a truly deserving member of the titin protein family.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the measured length of Sallimus.

claim: Long titin family members with extensive elastic domains were found in the claw muscles of crayfish that contain extensively long sarcomeres
source: Similarly, long titin family members with extensive elastic domains were also found in the claw muscles of crayfish (as Drosophila an arthropod) that contain extensively long sarcomeres (Fukuzawa et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: C. elegans contains a Sallimus homolog called TTN-1 that is a 2 MDa protein spanning across the I-band
source: Importantly, also C. elegans contains a Sallimus homolog called TTN-1. TTN-1 is a 2 MDa protein that spans across the I-band and was thus also suggested to mechanically link the Z-disc to the myosin filaments in C. elegans body muscles (Forbes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: About eight or nine approximately 250-nm long Projectin molecules would be needed to bridge half the myosin filament if they do not overlap much
source: If they do not overlap much, about eight or nine ~250-nm long Projectin molecules (Schueder et al., 2023) would be needed to bridge half the myosin filament.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from measurements and geometric calculations.

claim: The theoretical length of a chain of about 70 folded Ig and Fn domains is consistent with the number of Projectin molecules needed to bridge half the myosin filament
source: This is consistent with the theoretical length of a chain of about 70 folded Ig and Fn domains, each about 4 nm (Mayans et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Projectin decorates the entire thick filament of likely all Drosophila muscles, except indirect flight muscles
source: The fact that Projectin decorates the entire thick filament of likely all Drosophila muscles, except indirect flight muscles, has the interesting consequence that the Projectin kinase is also located along the entire thick filament.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: C. elegans Projectin homolog Twitchin also decorates the entire thick filament
source: The same is true for the C. elegans Projectin homolog called Twitchin (Forbes et al., 2010), so Drosophila Projectin is not the exception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Titin kinases, including the Projectin kinase, are possibly modulated by mechanical stretch
source: Titin kinases, including the Projectin kinase, are possibly modulated by mechanical stretch: an inhibitory C-terminal tail needs to be pulled out of the kinase domain to allow kinase activity (Gautel, 2011; Gräter et al., 2005; Kobe et al., 1996; Lange et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on titin kinase regulation.

claim: A kinase-dead variant of C. elegans Twitchin results in normal sarcomere morphology but abnormally strong muscle contractions
source: Thus far, this has been tested in C. elegans: a kinase-dead variant of Twitchin results in normal sarcomere morphology but abnormally strong muscle contractions that lead to an evolutionary disadvantage (Matsunaga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.
